decks.title: Circular Flow of Income — Part 1: The Two-Sector Model
goals: Explain the circular flow of income and why it never stops
Draw the two-sector model with its real and money flows in the factor and product markets
Show how saving and investment through the financial market keep the flow steady

slides.heading: Circular Flow of Income
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **production, income and spending** moving in a circle between **households and firms**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what the circle is, the simple two-sector model, real and money flows, saving and investment, and why it matters
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every rupee you spend becomes someone else's income, and that income is spent again. Economists picture this as a circle that never stops. In this part we draw the simplest version of that circle, with only households and firms, and then see what happens when families begin to save.

slides.heading: What is the circular flow of income?
slides.body_md: Firms **produce**, production creates **income** for the owners of factors, income is **spent** on output, and spending lets firms **produce again**.

visual.alt: Flow of the circle: production by firms creates income for factor owners, income is spent on output, and spending calls forth more production
visual.caption: Production, income, spending

slides.narration: The circular flow is the endless movement of production, income and spending. Firms make goods and pay the people who supply land, labour, capital and enterprise. Those people spend their earnings on what firms make. That spending gives firms the money to produce and pay incomes again, so the flow goes round and round.

slides.heading: Assumptions of the simple model
slides.body_md: We begin with the **simplest possible economy** and add features one at a time.

rows: Firms sell all output to households
Firms pay all output value as factor incomes

visual.alt: Table of the assumptions of the simple two-sector model: only households and firms, all income spent, all output sold to households, and households own all the factors

slides.narration: To start, we imagine an economy with only two sectors, households and firms. There is no government and no trade with other countries. Households own all the factors and spend everything they earn, and firms sell all their output to households. Later we will relax these assumptions one by one.

slides.heading: The two-sector model
slides.body_md: Two markets, four flows: two **real**, two **money**.

Real flows are solid and money flows are dashed; each money flow runs opposite to the real flow it pays for.
visual.caption: Two-sector model, no saving: the top two flows are in the factor market, the bottom two in the product market.

slides.narration: Here is the picture. In the factor market, households supply factor services to firms and receive rent, wages, interest and profit. In the product market, firms supply goods and services to households and receive consumption spending. The solid lines are real flows and the dashed lines are money flows. Notice that each payment travels against the thing it pays for.

slides.heading: Quick check: is a bank needed?
slides.body_md: True or false: with no saving at all, a financial market is needed to keep income flowing.
slides.narration: Think about where every rupee of household income goes when nothing is saved.

slides.heading: Real flows and money flows
columns:
**Real flows**

- Factor services to firms
- Goods and services to households
- Things that are produced or used

**Money flows**

- Factor payments to households
- Consumption spending to firms
- Rupees that pay for the real flows

rows: Labour, land, capital, enterprise to firms
Rent, wages, interest, profit to households

visual.alt: Table comparing real and money flows in the factor and product markets: real flows carry factor services and goods; money flows carry payments in the opposite direction

slides.narration: A real flow is a movement of things: work, the use of land and machines, and finished goods. A money flow is the movement of rupees that pays for them. Because every real flow is paid for at its price, the money flows have the same value as the real flows, but they run the other way.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: incomes on an imagined island
slides.body_md: Kanakdwip firms pay wages, rent, interest and profit. Households save nothing. Find income and consumption.
bullets: Step 1 — Add the factor payments: 500 + 80 + 70 + 150 = **800** (₹ crore).
Step 2 — This is household income, because households own every factor.
Step 3 — With no saving, all of it is spent: consumption = **800**.
Step 4 — Firms get back exactly what they paid out, so the flow repeats.

visual.alt: Table of imagined Kanakdwip: wages 500, rent 80, interest 70 and profit 150 crore rupees add to household income of 800 crore, all of which is spent
visual.caption: Imagined island economy with no saving.

slides.narration: On our imagined island, firms pay five hundred crore in wages, eighty in rent, seventy in interest and one hundred and fifty in profit. Together that is eight hundred crore of household income. Families save nothing, so all eight hundred crore comes back to firms as spending, and the circle repeats at the same size.

slides.heading: Quick check: add the factor incomes
slides.body_md: Kanakdwip firms pay wages, rent, interest and profit. What is household income?
slides.narration: Profit is a factor payment too, so include every one of the four rewards.

slides.heading: One round of the circle
slides.body_md: The circle has no beginning or end; we simply pick a starting point.

visual.alt: Flow of one round of the two-sector circle: households supply factors, firms produce, firms pay factor incomes, households buy output, and firms hire factors again
visual.caption: One round

slides.narration: Follow one round. Households supply their factors. Firms use them to produce. Firms pay factor incomes. Households spend those incomes on the output. With that money, firms can hire factors again. Because each step leads to the next, the flow continues as long as nothing leaks out of it.

slides.heading: Two markets in the circle
slides.body_md: In the **factor market** households sell; in the **product market** firms sell.

visual.alt: Table of the two markets of the circular flow: in the factor market households sell factor services to firms for rent, wages, interest and profit; in the product market firms sell goods and services to households for consumption spending

slides.narration: The circle passes through two markets. In the factor market, households are the sellers and firms the buyers of factor services. In the product market, it is the other way round: firms sell goods and households buy them. The same households and firms play both roles.

slides.heading: Quick check: put the round in order
slides.body_md: Arrange one round of the two-sector circle in the correct order.
slides.narration: Start with what households offer, and end with what they buy.

slides.heading: When households save
slides.body_md: **Saving** is income not spent on consumer goods. The **financial market** lends it to firms as **investment**.

When investment equals saving, firms receive as much as they paid out.
visual.caption: Money flows only. Imagined Neelachal: income 900, saving 140, investment 140 (₹ crore).

slides.narration: Now let families save part of their income. That saving does not reach firms as consumer spending, so firms would be short of money. But savings go to banks and other institutions, which lend them to firms. Firms spend the loans on machines, buildings and stocks. If investment equals saving, firms still receive all that they paid out.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: saving and investment in imagined Neelachal
slides.body_md: Income ₹900 crore; saving ₹140 crore; investment ₹140 crore. Does the flow stay the same?
bullets: Step 1 — Consumption = 900 − 140 = **760**.
Step 2 — Saving of 140 reaches firms through banks as investment of 140.
Step 3 — Firms receive 760 + 140 = **900**, equal to income.
Step 4 — Saving equals investment, so the flow stays the same size.

visual.alt: Table of imagined Neelachal: income 900, saving 140, consumption 760, investment 140; firms receive 900 crore rupees, equal to income
visual.caption: Saving returns as investment, so receipts equal income.

slides.narration: In imagined Neelachal, households earn nine hundred crore and save one hundred and forty, so they spend seven hundred and sixty. Banks lend the one hundred and forty crore to firms, which invest it. Firms therefore receive seven hundred and sixty plus one hundred and forty, which is nine hundred crore, exactly what they paid out.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the market
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank: household saving is lent to firms through the ___ market.
slides.narration: Think of the banks and institutions that collect deposits and give loans.

slides.heading: Why the circular flow matters
slides.body_md: It shows that national income can be measured at **three points** of one circle, that sectors **depend on each other**, and how **leakages and injections** change income.

visual.alt: Flow of three points where the circular flow can be measured: value of output by the product method, factor incomes by the income method, and spending on output by the expenditure method
visual.caption: Three points, one total

slides.narration: The circle is more than a picture. Because the same rupees pass through production, factor incomes and spending, national income can be measured in three ways that must agree. It also shows that a cut in one group's spending cuts another group's income, and it prepares us for leakages and injections in the next part.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: The circular flow is the unending movement of **production, income and spending**.
Two markets: **factor** and **product**; four flows, two real and two money, in opposite directions.
Money flows equal real flows in value.
With saving, the flow stays steady when **investment equals saving**.

slides.narration: Let us sum up. Production creates income, income is spent, and spending calls forth more production. In the simple model, factor services and goods move one way while payments move the other. When families save, the financial market returns their saving to firms as investment, and the flow stays steady if the two are equal.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Label **every arrow** in a circular-flow diagram and say whether it is real or money.
Money flows run **opposite** to real flows; do not draw them the same way.
Profit is a **factor payment** to households, not something kept outside the circle.
With saving, state the condition: **saving equals investment**.
slides.narration: Four habits earn marks here. Label each arrow and mark it as a real or a money flow. Draw money flows opposite to the real flows they pay for. Remember that profit goes to households as owners of enterprise. And when saving appears, always state that the flow is steady only if investment equals saving.

slides.narration: Real economies have governments that tax and spend, and they trade with other countries. In this part we add both to our circle. We then sort every flow into leakages, which take money out of the circle, and injections, which put money back, and see why income rises or falls when the two do not match.

slides.narration: Add the government at the top. Households and firms pay taxes to it. slides.heading: Purchases and transfers
columns:
**Government purchase**

- Buses, desks, medicines
- Goods come in return
- Has a matching real flow

**Transfer payment**

- Pensions, scholarships
- Nothing in return
- No matching real flow

visual.alt: Table comparing a government purchase with a transfer payment: a purchase brings goods in return and has a matching real flow; a transfer has nothing in return

slides.narration: Not all government payments are alike. When the state buys buses from a firm, the buses come in return, so there is a real flow opposite to the payment. When it pays a pension or a scholarship, nothing is produced or given back. Such transfer payments move income from one group to another without any matching real flow.

slides.heading: Quick check: a scholarship
slides.body_md: True or false: a government scholarship to a student is a money flow from the government to households.
slides.narration: Ask who pays, who receives, and whether anything comes back in return.

Step 3 — Injections = investment + government spending = 130 + 220 = **350**.
Step 4 — Equal, so firms receive 650 + 130 + 220 = 1,000: the flow is steady.

Firms receive one thousand crore, the same as income, so the flow is steady.

slides.narration: Now open the economy. Foreign buyers pay domestic firms for exports, which brings money into the circle. When households, firms or the government buy goods from abroad, the payments leave the country. So exports add to spending on our output, while imports take spending away from it.

slides.heading: Quick check: the fourth sector
slides.body_md: Fill in the blank: the four-sector model adds the ___ sector, which buys our exports and sells us imports.
slides.narration: Think of everyone outside the country who trades with it.

slides.heading: Leakages and injections
slides.body_md: A **leakage** takes income out of spending on domestic output; an **injection** adds spending from outside household consumption.

visual.alt: Table pairing leakages and injections by sector: saving and investment through the financial market, taxes and government spending through the government, imports and exports through the rest of the world

slides.narration: There are three leakages: saving, taxes and imports. There are three matching injections: investment, government spending and exports. Each pair passes through one place: saving and investment through the financial market, taxes and government spending through the government, and imports and exports through the rest of the world.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: an open economy in balance
slides.body_md: Imagined Vindhyadesh: compare total leakages with total injections.
bullets: Step 4 — Spending on domestic output = 800 + 180 + 260 + 110 − 150 = **1,200** = income.

visual.alt: Table of imagined Vindhyadesh: leakages of saving 160, taxes 240 and imports 150 total 550; injections of investment 180, government spending 260 and exports 110 total 550 crore rupees
visual.caption: Income 1,200; consumption 800; spending on domestic output 1,200.

slides.narration: In imagined Vindhyadesh, income is one thousand two hundred crore. Saving, taxes and imports total five hundred and fifty, and so do investment, government spending and exports. A second check agrees: consumption plus investment plus government spending plus exports, minus imports, comes back to one thousand two hundred. The flow is in balance.

slides.heading: Quick check: sort the flows
slides.body_md: Match each item with its place in the circular flow.
slides.narration: For each item, ask whether money is leaving the circle or coming into it, and through which sector.

slides.heading: When leakages exceed injections
slides.body_md: Less spending comes back than firms paid out, so **income falls**.

nodes.label: Income falls until leakages match injections

visual.alt: Flow of what happens when leakages exceed injections: spending falls short of output, unsold stocks pile up, firms cut output and jobs, and income falls until leakages match injections
visual.caption: Leakages larger

slides.narration: Suppose people plan to save, pay tax and import more than firms invest, the government spends and foreigners buy. Then firms receive less than they paid out. Goods stay unsold, so firms cut output and jobs, and income falls. As income falls, leakages shrink too, until they match injections again at a lower income.

The fifty crore gap means firms receive less than they paid out. Warehouses fill up, factories cut shifts, and income falls until leakages shrink to the level of injections.

slides.heading: When injections exceed leakages
slides.body_md: More spending comes back than firms paid out, so **income rises**.

nodes.label: Income rises until leakages match injections

visual.alt: Flow of what happens when injections exceed leakages: spending exceeds output, stocks run down, firms raise output and hire, and income rises until leakages match injections
visual.caption: Injections larger

slides.narration: Now the opposite case. If investment, government spending and exports are larger than saving, taxes and imports, firms receive more than they paid out. Their stocks run down, so they produce more and hire more workers. Income rises, and as it rises leakages grow, until they catch up with injections at a higher income.

slides.heading: Quick check: are exports a leakage?
slides.body_md: True or false: exports are a leakage because goods leave the country.
slides.narration: Follow the money, not the goods: which way does payment for exports travel?

slides.heading: Conditions for a steady flow
slides.body_md: In every model, the flow is steady when **total leakages equal total injections**.

rows: Saving + taxes + imports = investment + government spending + exports

visual.alt: Table of the condition for a steady circular flow in each model: saving equals investment in two sectors; saving plus taxes equals investment plus government spending in three; and saving plus taxes plus imports equals investment plus government spending plus exports in four

slides.narration: The rule is the same in every model; only the list grows. With saving alone, saving must equal investment. With a government, saving and taxes must equal investment and government spending. With foreign trade too, saving, taxes and imports must equal investment, government spending and exports.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: The **government** takes taxes and returns purchases, salaries, transfers and subsidies.
The **rest of the world** brings export receipts in and takes import payments out.
Leakages: **saving, taxes, imports**. Injections: **investment, government spending, exports**.
Leakages larger: income **falls**. Injections larger: income **rises**. Equal: income is **steady**.

visual.alt: Table pairing leakages and injections by sector: saving and investment through the financial market, taxes and government spending through the government, imports and exports through the rest of the world

slides.narration: To sum up, the government and the rest of the world each add a pair of flows to the circle. Saving, taxes and imports leak money out, while investment, government spending and exports inject it back. When the two sides are equal, income is steady; when one side is larger, income moves until they match again.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: **Imports are a leakage** and **exports an injection**: follow the money, not the goods.
Taxes are a leakage even though the government spends them: count that spending as an **injection**.
In numericals, list leakages and injections in two columns before adding.
Say **in which direction income moves** and **why** it stops moving.
slides.narration: Watch four points. Imports take money out and exports bring it in, whatever happens to the goods. Taxes are a leakage, and the government's spending is the matching injection. In calculations, set out leakages and injections side by side. And when they differ, explain both the direction of change in income and why it settles.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and importance of the circular flow
sections.body_md:
- **Circular flow of income**: the continuous movement of **production, income and expenditure** between the sectors of an economy. Production creates factor incomes, incomes are spent, and spending allows production to continue.
- It is circular because it **has no beginning or end**: one sector's spending is another sector's income.
- **Importance**: (1) national income can be measured at **three points** (product, income and expenditure methods), which must give the same total; (2) it shows the **interdependence** of sectors; (3) it identifies **leakages and injections**, which explain changes in income and guide policy.

key_terms.definition_md: The continuous movement of production, income and spending among the sectors of an economy.
Each sector depends on the spending of others for its income.

sections.heading: 2. The simple two-sector model
sections.body_md:
- **Assumptions**: only households and firms; no government; no foreign trade; households spend all income (no saving); firms sell all output to households; households own all factors.
- **Factor market**: households supply land, labour, capital and enterprise (real flow) and receive rent, wages, interest and profit (money flow).
- **Product market**: firms supply goods and services (real flow) and receive consumption spending (money flow).
- **Real flows** are flows of factor services and goods; **money flows** are payments. They move in **opposite directions** and are **equal in value**.
- Imagined Kanakdwip: wages 500 + rent 80 + interest 70 + profit 150 = ₹800 crore of income, all spent.

A flow of payments, such as factor incomes or consumption spending.
The market where households sell factor services to firms.
The market where firms sell goods and services to households.

sections.heading: 3. Saving, investment and the financial market
sections.body_md:
- When households **save**, consumer spending is less than income, so firms' receipts fall short.
- The **financial (capital) market**, made up of banks and other institutions, collects saving and **lends it to firms**, which spend it on **investment** (machines, buildings, stocks).
- **Condition for a steady flow**: **investment = saving**. If investment is less than saving, income shrinks; if it is more, income grows.
- Imagined Neelachal: income 900, saving 140, consumption 760, investment 140; receipts 900 = income (₹ crore).

key_terms.definition_md: The part of income not spent on consumption.
Spending by firms on capital goods and stocks.
Banks and institutions that channel saving into loans for investment.

sections.heading: 4. The three-sector model: adding the government
sections.body_md:
- Households and firms pay **taxes** to the government (a leakage).
- The government pays **salaries** and factor incomes to households, **transfers** such as pensions and scholarships, buys **goods and services** from firms, and pays **subsidies** to firms (government spending, an injection).
- A **purchase** has goods in return; a **transfer** has nothing in return.
- Household budget: income = consumption + saving + taxes. Example: income 900, taxes 150, saving 120, so consumption 630 (₹ crore).
- **Condition for a steady flow**: saving + taxes = investment + government spending. Imagined Malaygiri: 150 + 200 = 130 + 220 = 350.

sections.heading: 6. Leakages and injections
sections.body_md:
- **Leakages (withdrawals)**: income not passed on as spending on domestic output: **saving, taxes, imports**.
- **Injections**: spending added from outside household consumption: **investment, government spending, exports**.
- **Leakages larger than injections**: spending falls short of output, stocks pile up, firms cut output, **income falls** until leakages shrink to match. Imagined Sarayu Pradesh: 520 against 470, a gap of 50 (₹ crore).
- **Injections larger than leakages**: stocks run down, firms raise output, **income rises** until leakages grow to match. Imagined Tungadesh: 310 against 280.
- At every level of the model, income is steady when **total leakages = total injections**.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Drawing money flows in the same direction as real flows.
- Calling imports an injection because goods come in, or exports a leakage because goods go out.
- Forgetting that profit is a factor income of households.
- Subtracting only saving (or only taxes) when finding consumption in the three-sector model.
- Stating a direction of change in income without the reason (unsold stocks or running-down stocks).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a correct option, a classification or a one-step calculation.
- 2 marks: two points, or a point with an example.
- 3 marks: three points, or a calculation with a conclusion.
- 5 marks (and ISC 4- and 8-mark questions): a labelled explanation or diagram description in parts, with working and a reasoned conclusion.

cards.back_md: A **leakage**; the government's spending is counted separately as an **injection**.

questions.stem_md: A student in an imagined Shillong classroom is asked to define the circular flow of income. Which definition is correct?

options.text_md: The one-way movement of goods from factories to shops
The unending movement of production, income and spending between the sectors of an economy
The total value of goods kept in a firm's warehouse on a given date
The yearly increase in the money supply of a country

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The unending movement of production, income and spending between the sectors of an economy. The circular flow shows production creating income, income being spent, and spending calling forth more production, round and round. A one-way movement of goods leaves out income and spending; a stock in a warehouse is a stock, not a flow; money supply is a different idea.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is an assumption of the simplest two-sector model of the circular flow, used for the imagined island of Kanakdwip?

options.text_md: Firms pay taxes to the government on their profits
Households buy some goods from foreign countries
Firms keep part of their receipts as saving in banks
Households spend their entire income on goods and services produced by firms

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Households spend their entire income on goods and services produced by firms. The simplest model has only households and firms, no government, no foreign trade and no saving, so all income is spent on firms' output. Taxes need a government, imports need a foreign sector, and saving is added only in the extended two-sector model.

questions.stem_md: In imagined Kanakdwip, which of these is a real flow from households to firms?

options.text_md: A carpenter's labour supplied to a furniture firm
Wages paid by the furniture firm to the carpenter
Rupees a family spends on a new dining table
Profit paid out by the firm to its owner

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A carpenter's labour supplied to a furniture firm. Real flows are flows of factor services and goods. The carpenter's labour is a factor service moving from a household to a firm. Wages, consumption spending and profit are all money flows.

questions.stem_md: A bakery in an imagined hill town pays rent to the family that owns its shop. In the circular flow this rent is

options.text_md: a real flow from firms to households, as goods
a money flow from households to firms, as consumption spending
a money flow from firms to households, as a factor payment
a real flow from households to firms, as labour

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a money flow from firms to households, as a factor payment. Rent is the reward for the land and building that the family (a household) lets to the bakery (a firm), so it is a factor payment, a money flow from firms to households.

questions.stem_md: How do the real flows and the money flows of the two-sector circular flow move relative to each other?

options.text_md: In the same direction
Real flows move only in the factor market
In opposite directions
Money flows move only in the product market

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** In opposite directions. Every real flow is paid for: labour goes from households to firms while wages come back from firms to households, and goods go to households while spending goes to firms. So the two flows run in opposite directions in both markets.

questions.stem_md: Firms in imagined Kanakdwip pay wages ₹500 crore, rent ₹80 crore, interest ₹70 crore and profit ₹150 crore. Households save nothing. What is total consumption expenditure on firms' output?

options.text_md: ₹800 crore
₹500 crore
₹650 crore
₹1600 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹800 crore. Total factor income = 500 + 80 + 70 + 150 = 800. With no saving, households spend all of it, so consumption expenditure is ₹800 crore. Wages alone or income without profit leave out factor payments; doubling counts the same rupees twice.

questions.stem_md: Households in imagined Neelachal save part of their income in banks. Through which channel does this saving return to firms in the extended two-sector model?

options.text_md: The government, which collects it as taxes
The rest of the world, which buys exports with it
The product market, where it is spent on consumer goods
The financial market, which lends it to firms for investment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The financial market, which lends it to firms for investment. Banks and other institutions of the financial (capital) market collect household saving and lend it to firms, which spend it on investment goods. Government and the foreign sector are not part of a two-sector model; saving is by definition not spent on consumer goods.

questions.stem_md: In imagined Neelachal, income is ₹900 crore and households save ₹140 crore. For the flow of income to stay at ₹900 crore, investment spending by firms must be

options.text_md: ₹760 crore
₹140 crore
₹900 crore
zero

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹140 crore. Consumption is 900 − 140 = 760. Firms receive 760 from consumers, so they need 140 more from investment spending to match the income they paid out. Saving must equal investment: ₹140 crore.

questions.stem_md: Why does a statistician in an imagined state planning office find the circular flow useful when estimating national income?

options.text_md: It shows that income can be measured at three points: production, distribution as factor incomes, and spending
It proves that every household has the same income
It shows that prices never change in an economy
It shows that firms make no profit in the long run

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It shows that income can be measured at three points: production, distribution as factor incomes, and spending. Because the same flow passes through production, factor incomes and expenditure, national income can be measured by the product, income and expenditure methods, and all three must agree. The other statements are not implied by the circular flow.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a two-sector economy without saving, consumption expenditure equals the factor payments made by firms.

Choose the correct option.

Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since nothing is saved, every rupee paid out as wages, rent, interest and profit comes back to firms as spending on their output.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Real flows and money flows in the circular flow move in opposite directions.

**Reason (R):** The value of the money flows equals the value of the real flows.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. The flows run opposite because payment travels against the goods or services bought; the equality of values is a separate fact about the size of the flows, not their direction.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the simplest two-sector model, where households save nothing, a financial market is needed to keep income flowing.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** False. With no saving, all income is spent on firms' goods, so nothing needs to be channelled back. The financial market is needed only when households save and firms invest.

questions.stem_md: In the extended two-sector model, the market in which household saving is lent to firms for investment is called the ___ market.
questions.solution_md: It is the financial (or capital) market: banks and other institutions that turn household saving into loans for investment.

questions.stem_md: Firms in imagined Kanakdwip pay wages ₹500 crore, rent ₹80 crore, interest ₹70 crore and profit ₹150 crore. What is the total factor income of households (in ₹ crore)?
questions.solution_md: Total factor income = 500 + 80 + 70 + 150 = 800, that is ₹800 crore.

questions.stem_md: Match each event in an imagined handloom town with the flow it represents in the two-sector model.

options.text_md: A weaver works a full day at a cloth mill
The mill pays the weaver her daily wage
A family carries home a bale of cloth
The family pays the shop for the cloth

questions.stem_md: Arrange one round of the two-sector circular flow of imagined Kanakdwip in the correct order, starting with households.

options.text_md: Households spend this income on goods and services from firms
Households supply land, labour, capital and enterprise to firms
Firms pay rent, wages, interest and profit to households
Firms use these factors to produce goods and services

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a real flow from a money flow, giving one example of each from a village pottery business.
questions.solution_md: Goods and services versus payments, each with an example.

answer.model_answer_md: A **real flow** is a movement of **factor services or goods**, for example a potter's labour going to the pottery unit or pots going to buyers. A **money flow** is a movement of **payments**, for example the potter's wages or the rupees buyers pay for pots.

questions.stem_md: State two assumptions on which the simple two-sector circular flow model of an imagined island economy is built.
questions.solution_md: Any two: two sectors only; no government; closed economy; no saving; all output sold to households.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. There are only **two sectors**, households and firms: **no government** and **no foreign trade**.
2. Households **spend all their income** on goods produced by firms, so there is **no saving**, and firms sell all they produce to households.

questions.stem_md: Households in imagined Neelachal start saving part of their income. Explain how the financial market keeps the flow of income from shrinking.
questions.solution_md: Saving is a withdrawal; the financial market returns it as investment.

answer.model_answer_md: Saving is income **not spent** on consumer goods, so firms' sales would fall short. Banks collect this saving and **lend it to firms**, which spend it on **investment** goods. If investment equals saving, total spending again equals income.

questions.stem_md: Give three reasons why the circular flow of income is useful for a planner studying an imagined state economy.
questions.solution_md: Measurement, interdependence, and leakages and injections for policy.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Measuring national income**: the flow can be measured at production, at factor incomes or at spending, giving the three methods.
2. **Interdependence**: it shows that households and firms depend on each other, so a fall in one sector's spending cuts another's income.
3. **Leakages and injections**: it shows how saving, taxes and imports withdraw money and how investment, government spending and exports return it, which guides policy.

questions.stem_md: Describe the four flows of the simple two-sector model of an imagined economy, saying in which market each flow takes place.
questions.solution_md: Two flows in each market, real and money, in opposite directions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Factor market, real**: households supply land, labour, capital and enterprise to firms.
2. **Factor market, money**: firms pay rent, wages, interest and profit to households.
3. **Product market, real**: firms supply goods and services to households.
4. **Product market, money**: households pay firms for these goods as consumption spending. Each money flow runs opposite to the real flow it pays for.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Neelachal has income of ₹900 crore; households save ₹140 crore and firms invest ₹140 crore. Show with these figures that the flow of income continues unchanged.
questions.solution_md: Consumption, saving returned as investment, receipts equal income.

answer.model_answer_md: Households spend 900 − 140 = **₹760 crore** on consumer goods. The saving of ₹140 crore reaches firms through banks and is spent as **investment of ₹140 crore**. Firms therefore receive 760 + 140 = **₹900 crore**, exactly the income they paid out, so they can pay the same incomes again and the flow does not shrink.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about the two-sector economy of an imagined island. [2 + 3]

(a) Distinguish the factor market from the product market in the circular flow. [2]
(b) Explain how the circular flow works when households save part of their income, and state the condition for the flow to stay unchanged. [3]
questions.solution_md: Two markets; saving returned through the financial market; S = I.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In the **factor market**, households sell the services of land, labour, capital and enterprise to firms and receive rent, wages, interest and profit. In the **product market**, firms sell goods and services to households and receive consumption spending.
(b) When households **save** part of their income, consumer spending falls short of the income firms paid out, so firms' receipts would fall. The saving is deposited with **banks and other financial institutions**, which **lend it to firms**. Firms spend these funds on machines, buildings and stocks, that is, **investment**. If **investment equals saving**, the money withdrawn as saving returns in full, firms receive as much as they paid, and the flow continues at the **same level**. If investment is smaller, income shrinks.

marking_scheme.step: Financial market returns it as investment

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 3]

(a) Why are the money flows in a two-sector economy without saving equal in value to the real flows? [2]
(b) Using the circular flow, explain why national income measured by output, by factor incomes and by expenditure gives the same total. [3]
questions.solution_md: Payment for every real flow; one flow measured at three points.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Every real flow is **bought and paid for**. Factor services are paid at their price as rent, wages, interest and profit, and goods are paid for at their price by consumers. So the value of what moves one way equals the money that moves the other way.
(b) The value of goods produced by firms is **entirely paid out** to the owners of the factors as rent, wages, interest and profit, because profit is whatever is left after other payments. So **output equals factor income**. Households then **spend all** of that income on the same goods, so **income equals expenditure**. The same rupees are counted at three points of one circle, which is why the **product, income and expenditure methods** must give the same national income.

marking_scheme.step: Every real flow is paid for

questions.stem_md: In the three-sector circular flow of imagined Malaygiri, which of these is a money flow from the government to households?

options.text_md: Income tax paid by a doctor
An old-age pension paid to a retired farmer
Sales tax collected on a television
Payment for imported crude oil

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** An old-age pension paid to a retired farmer. A pension is a transfer payment from the government to a household. Income tax and sales tax flow the other way, to the government; oil imports involve the rest of the world, not the three-sector model.

questions.stem_md: A teacher extends the two-sector circular flow of an imagined country into a three-sector model. Which sector is added?

options.text_md: The rest of the world
The financial market
The government
The banking sector only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The government. The three-sector model adds the government, with taxes, government purchases, transfers and subsidies. The rest of the world is the fourth sector; the financial market already appears in the extended two-sector model.

questions.stem_md: A leather firm in an imagined Kanpur sells shoes to buyers in Europe. In the four-sector circular flow, the payment it receives is

options.text_md: a money flow from domestic firms to the rest of the world
a money flow from the government to firms
a real flow from the rest of the world to households
a money flow from the rest of the world to domestic firms

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a money flow from the rest of the world to domestic firms. Export receipts come into the country from foreign buyers, so they flow from the rest of the world to domestic firms. Payments going abroad are for imports; the government and households are not involved here.

questions.stem_md: A family in an imagined Kerala town buys a mobile phone made abroad. In the four-sector model this purchase creates

options.text_md: a money flow from the rest of the world to domestic firms
a money flow from households to the government
a money flow from domestic firms to households
a money flow from the domestic economy to the rest of the world

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a money flow from the domestic economy to the rest of the world. The rupees paid for an imported good go to foreign producers, so they leave the domestic flow for the rest of the world. That is why imports are a leakage.

questions.stem_md: The imagined government of Malaygiri pays a subsidy to fertiliser firms. In the three-sector model this is

options.text_md: a money flow from firms to the government
a real flow from firms to the government
a money flow from the government to firms
a money flow from households to the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a money flow from the government to firms. A subsidy is a payment made by the government to producers, so money moves from the government to firms. Taxes are the flow in the other direction.

questions.stem_md: In a three-sector model of an imagined economy, households earn ₹900 crore, pay taxes of ₹150 crore and save ₹120 crore. How much do they spend on consumer goods?

options.text_md: ₹780 crore
₹630 crore
₹750 crore
₹900 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** ₹630 crore. Household income is used for consumption, saving and taxes, so C = 900 − 150 − 120 = 630. Subtracting only one of the two withdrawals overstates consumption.

questions.stem_md: The imagined state of Malaygiri buys desks for its schools from a furniture firm. Which pair of flows does this create?

options.text_md: A real flow of desks from the firm to the government and a money flow of payment from the government to the firm
A money flow of taxes from the firm to the government and nothing in return
A real flow of desks from households to the government
A transfer payment from the government to households

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A real flow of desks from the firm to the government and a money flow of payment from the government to the firm. A government purchase is an exchange: goods go to the government and payment goes to the firm, in opposite directions. A tax or a transfer has no goods or service in return.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Taxes are a leakage from the circular flow of income.

**Reason (R):** Taxes collected by the government are never spent again in the economy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: taxes are income taken out of households' and firms' spending. R is false: the government spends tax revenue on purchases, salaries and transfers, which is why government spending appears as an injection.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the three-sector model, a scholarship paid by the government to a student is a money flow from the government to households.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** True. A scholarship is a transfer payment from the government to a household, with no good or service given in return.

questions.stem_md: The four-sector model adds the ___ sector, which buys a country's exports and sells it imports.
questions.solution_md: The fourth sector is the rest of the world (the foreign or external sector).

questions.stem_md: In the three-sector economy of imagined Gomtipur, taxes are ₹90 crore, investment ₹120 crore and government spending ₹110 crore. What saving would keep the flow of income in balance (in ₹ crore)?
questions.solution_md: Balance needs S + T = I + G, so S = 120 + 110 − 90 = 140, that is ₹140 crore.

questions.stem_md: Households in imagined Vindhyadesh earn ₹1,200 crore, save ₹160 crore and pay taxes of ₹240 crore. What is their consumption expenditure (in ₹ crore)?
State the two money flows between the government and households in the three-sector circular flow of an imagined state, with an example of each.
questions.solution_md: Taxes one way; transfers and wages the other.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Households to the government**: **taxes**, for example income tax paid by a shopkeeper.
2. **Government to households**: **transfers and factor payments**, for example an old-age pension or the salary of a government school teacher.

questions.stem_md: Name the two money flows that link the domestic economy with the rest of the world in the four-sector model, giving an example of each from an imagined port city.
questions.solution_md: Exports bring money in; imports send money out.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Export receipts**: money flows **into** the country, for example foreign buyers paying a port city firm for shrimp.
2. **Import payments**: money flows **out**, for example a refinery in the city paying a foreign supplier for crude oil.

questions.stem_md: The imagined government of Malaygiri pays a widow's pension and also buys buses from a local firm. Explain why only one of these comes with a real flow.
questions.solution_md: Purchase is an exchange; transfer has no counterpart.

answer.model_answer_md: The **bus purchase** is an exchange: buses (a real flow) go to the government while payment goes to the firm. The **pension** is a **transfer payment**: money goes to the widow but **nothing is produced or given in return**, so there is no matching real flow.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Malaygiri has income ₹1,000 crore, saving ₹150 crore, taxes ₹200 crore, investment ₹130 crore and government spending ₹220 crore. Find consumption and show that the flow is in balance.
questions.solution_md: Consumption, then leakages against injections, then spending against income.

answer.model_answer_md: Consumption = 1000 − 150 − 200 = **₹650 crore**. Leakages = saving + taxes = 150 + 200 = **₹350 crore**; injections = investment + government spending = 130 + 220 = **₹350 crore**. They are **equal**, and firms receive 650 + 130 + 220 = ₹1,000 crore, the same as income, so the flow is in balance.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the four-sector model of an imagined trading nation extends the three-sector model of its circular flow.
questions.solution_md: Open economy; exports in; imports out; new balance condition.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It adds the **rest of the world** as a fourth sector, so the economy is **open**.
2. Domestic firms **export** goods and receive **export receipts**, which is an **injection** of money into the domestic flow.
3. Households, firms and the government **import** goods and make **import payments**, a **leakage** of money abroad. Balance now needs saving + taxes + imports = investment + government spending + exports.

marking_scheme.step: Imports as a leakage and the balance condition

questions.stem_md: Describe three ways in which the government of an imagined state takes part in the circular flow of income.
questions.solution_md: Taxes, purchases and factor payments, transfers and subsidies.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Collects taxes** from households and firms, which withdraws money from their spending.
2. **Buys goods and services** from firms and **hires factors**, such as teachers and road workers, paying them salaries; this returns money to the flow.
3. **Pays transfers and subsidies**, such as pensions to households and subsidies to fertiliser firms, which add to their spending power without any good in return.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about the circular flow of an imagined country. [2 + 3]

(a) What new flows appear when the government is added to the two-sector model? [2]
(b) Explain the flows that appear when the rest of the world is added, and how they change the condition for balance. [3]
questions.solution_md: Government flows; foreign flows; new balance condition.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Households and firms pay **taxes** to the government. The government pays **salaries** and **transfers** such as pensions to households, buys **goods and services** from firms, and pays **subsidies** to firms. Taxes withdraw money, while government spending returns it.
(b) With the **rest of the world**, domestic firms sell **exports** and receive export receipts, which bring money **into** the domestic flow. Households, firms and the government buy **imports** and send payments **abroad**, which take money **out** of it. Imports are therefore a **leakage** and exports an **injection**. Balance now requires **saving + taxes + imports = investment + government spending + exports**, and total spending on domestic output becomes consumption + investment + government spending + exports − imports.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about imagined Vindhyadesh (₹ crore): income 1,200, saving 160, taxes 240, imports 150, investment 180, government spending 260, exports 110. [2 + 3]

(a) Find household consumption. [2]
(b) Show that the flow is in balance by two methods: comparing leakages with injections, and comparing total spending on domestic output with income. [3]
questions.solution_md: Consumption; leakages equal injections; spending equals income.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Households use income for consumption, saving and taxes, so consumption = 1200 − 160 − 240 = **₹800 crore**.
(b) **Method 1**: leakages = saving + taxes + imports = 160 + 240 + 150 = **₹550 crore**; injections = investment + government spending + exports = 180 + 260 + 110 = **₹550 crore**. They are equal. **Method 2**: spending on domestic output = consumption + investment + government spending + exports − imports = 800 + 180 + 260 + 110 − 150 = **₹1,200 crore**, equal to income. Both methods show that every rupee withdrawn is returned, so income neither rises nor falls.

questions.stem_md: In the circular flow of an imagined country, a leakage is best described as

options.text_md: spending added to the flow from outside the household sector's consumption
income that is withdrawn from the flow instead of being spent on domestic output
a fall in the price of goods during a slump
the output that firms fail to sell in a year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** income that is withdrawn from the flow instead of being spent on domestic output. A leakage (withdrawal) is income not passed on as spending on domestic goods: saving, taxes and imports. Spending added from outside is an injection.

questions.stem_md: Which of these events in an imagined state is an injection into its circular flow of income?

options.text_md: A family deposits part of its income in a bank
A salaried worker pays income tax
A mill imports cotton from abroad
The state government builds a new district hospital

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The state government builds a new district hospital. Government spending on a hospital adds spending that does not come from household consumption, so it is an injection. Saving, taxes and imports are leakages.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a leakage from the circular flow of an imagined coastal economy?

options.text_md: Tax deducted from a teacher's salary
Purchase of a fishing trawler by a firm
Sale of dried fish to a foreign buyer
Construction of a jetty by the government

questions.stem_md: In imagined Sarayu Pradesh, planned leakages are ₹520 crore and planned injections ₹470 crore. What will happen to national income?

options.text_md: It will rise
It will stay the same
It will fall
It will double

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It will fall. Leakages exceed injections by ₹50 crore, so less money returns to firms as spending than they paid out. They cannot sell all their output, cut production and pay out less income, so national income falls until leakages and injections are equal again.

questions.stem_md: Which condition must hold for the flow of income of an imagined open economy with a government to stay at the same level?

options.text_md: Saving + investment = taxes + government spending
Exports + imports = saving + taxes
Saving + taxes + imports = investment + government spending + exports
Consumption = saving

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Saving + taxes + imports = investment + government spending + exports. In the four-sector model the leakages are saving, taxes and imports, and the injections are investment, government spending and exports. The flow is steady when total leakages equal total injections. The other options mix leakages with injections.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Konkanpur has saving ₹140 crore, taxes ₹160 crore, imports ₹120 crore, investment ₹150 crore and government spending ₹190 crore. What value of exports would keep its income steady?

options.text_md: ₹80 crore
₹120 crore
₹420 crore
₹40 crore

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** ₹80 crore. Leakages = 140 + 160 + 120 = 420. Injections other than exports = 150 + 190 = 340. Exports needed = 420 − 340 = 80.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Tungadesh plans leakages of ₹280 crore and injections of ₹310 crore. Which outcome is most likely if it has idle factories and workers?

options.text_md: Output and income fall
Income stays unchanged because the gap is small
Exports fall to zero
Output, income and employment rise

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Output, income and employment rise. Injections exceed leakages by ₹30 crore, so firms receive more spending than they paid out as income. With idle capacity they expand output and hire more workers, so income and employment rise until leakages catch up with injections.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a leakage from an injection in the circular flow, giving one example of each from an imagined farming district.
questions.solution_md: Withdrawal versus addition, with examples.

answer.model_answer_md: A **leakage** is income **withdrawn** from spending on domestic output, for example a farmer depositing part of his crop income in a bank. An **injection** is spending **added** from outside household consumption, for example the state building a canal in the district.

questions.stem_md: Exports of carpets from an imagined state rise while its saving, taxes and imports stay the same. Explain the likely effect on its income.
questions.solution_md: Injections exceed leakages, so income rises.

answer.model_answer_md: Exports are an **injection**, so injections now **exceed leakages**. Carpet makers receive more than they paid out, **expand output and hire more weavers**, and income **rises**. It keeps rising until higher saving, taxes and imports make leakages equal to injections.

marking_scheme.step: Exports are an injection; injections exceed leakages

questions.stem_md: State the condition for a steady flow of income in a three-sector economy and explain it briefly, with reference to an imagined state.
questions.solution_md: S + T = I + G, withdrawn money fully returned.

answer.model_answer_md: The condition is **saving + taxes = investment + government spending**. Saving and taxes are the money households and firms **withdraw**; investment and government spending are the money **returned**. When the two totals are equal, the state's income neither grows nor shrinks.

questions.stem_md: Imagined Sarayu Pradesh plans leakages of ₹520 crore and injections of ₹470 crore. Explain, step by step, what happens to its income.
questions.solution_md: Shortfall, cut in output, fall in income until balance.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Leakages exceed injections by **₹50 crore**, so firms receive **less spending** than the income they paid out.
2. Goods pile up **unsold**, so firms **cut production** and employ fewer workers.
3. Lower income reduces saving, tax payments and imports, so leakages **fall**. Income keeps **falling** until leakages again equal injections at a lower level.

marking_scheme.step: Income falls until leakages equal injections

questions.stem_md: Classify each item as a leakage or an injection for an imagined island economy: (i) a hotel chain builds a new resort, (ii) a fisherman saves in a cooperative bank, (iii) the island buys diesel from abroad, (iv) the government pays nurses' salaries, (v) a shopkeeper pays sales tax, (vi) coconut oil is sold to a foreign buyer.
questions.solution_md: Three injections and three leakages, each named.

answer.model_answer_md: **Injections**: (i) building a resort is **investment**; (iv) nurses' salaries are **government spending**; (vi) coconut oil sold abroad is an **export**. **Leakages**: (ii) the fisherman's deposit is **saving**; (iii) diesel bought abroad is an **import**; (v) sales tax is a **tax**. Each pair of leakages and injections matches one sector: households, the government and the rest of the world.

questions.stem_md: For imagined Konkanpur (₹ crore: saving 140, taxes 160, imports 120, investment 150, government spending 190), find the exports needed for balance and explain what happens if exports turn out lower.
questions.solution_md: Solve the balance condition; lower exports mean a fall in income.

answer.model_answer_md: Balance needs leakages = injections: 140 + 160 + 120 = 150 + 190 + exports, so 420 = 340 + exports and **exports = ₹80 crore**. If exports are lower, **leakages exceed injections**, firms receive less than they paid out, and **income falls** until leakages shrink to match.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about the circular flow of an imagined open economy. [2 + 3]

(a) Name the three leakages and the three injections, linking each to the sector where it occurs. [2]
(b) Explain what happens to national income when injections exceed leakages, and why the economy settles again. [3]
questions.solution_md: Three of each with sectors; rising income raises leakages until balance.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Leakages**: **saving** by households (through the financial market), **taxes** (to the government) and **imports** (to the rest of the world). **Injections**: **investment** by firms, **government spending** on goods, services and salaries, and **exports** bought by the rest of the world.
(b) When **injections exceed leakages**, firms receive **more spending** than the income they paid out, and their stocks run down. They **raise output** and hire more factors, so **incomes rise**. As incomes rise, households **save more**, pay **more taxes** and buy **more imports**, so leakages grow. Income keeps rising until **leakages equal injections** again, at a **higher** level of income, where the flow becomes steady.

marking_scheme.step: New balance at a higher income

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about imagined Sarayu Pradesh (₹ crore): saving 200, taxes 180, imports 140, investment 170, government spending 190, exports 110. [2 + 3]

(a) Calculate the gap between leakages and injections and state its direction. [2]
(b) Suggest and evaluate two ways in which the government could close this gap. [3]
questions.solution_md: Gap computed; two measures weighed.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Leakages = 200 + 180 + 140 = **₹520 crore**; injections = 170 + 190 + 110 = **₹470 crore**. Leakages **exceed** injections by **₹50 crore**, so income will tend to fall.
(b) **Raise government spending** by about ₹50 crore, for example on rural roads: this adds an injection directly and creates jobs, but it must be financed, and borrowing adds to public debt. **Cut taxes** to reduce a leakage: households keep more income and spend more, but part of the tax cut is saved, so a larger cut may be needed. Raising spending works **faster and more surely**, while a tax cut spreads the benefit more widely; a mix of the two is often the most practical choice.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both subparts about imagined Kanakdwip. [2 + 2]

(i) Firms pay wages ₹500 crore, rent ₹80 crore, interest ₹70 crore and profit ₹150 crore. With no saving, find household income and consumption spending.
(ii) Explain why profit is counted as a factor payment to households in the circular flow.
questions.solution_md: Sum of factor incomes; profit as the reward to entrepreneurs.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Household income = 500 + 80 + 70 + 150 = **₹800 crore**. With no saving, all of it is spent, so consumption spending = **₹800 crore**, the same as the value of firms' output.
(ii) Profit is the **reward for enterprise**, a factor service supplied by the owners of firms, who belong to the **household** sector. Firms pay out the whole value of output as rent, wages, interest and profit, so profit is the **remainder** that completes the payment to factor owners.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Reward for enterprise owned by households

questions.stem_md:
Answer both subparts about imagined Malaygiri. [2 + 2]

(i) Households earn ₹1,000 crore, save ₹150 crore and pay taxes of ₹200 crore. Find their consumption.
(ii) Firms invest ₹130 crore and the government spends ₹220 crore. Show whether the flow is in balance.
questions.solution_md: Consumption; leakages against injections.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Consumption = income − saving − taxes = 1000 − 150 − 200 = **₹650 crore**.
(ii) Leakages = 150 + 200 = **₹350 crore**; injections = 130 + 220 = **₹350 crore**. They are **equal**, so firms receive 650 + 130 + 220 = ₹1,000 crore, as much as they paid out, and the flow is in balance.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both subparts about imagined Tungadesh. [2 + 2]

(i) It plans saving ₹90 crore, taxes ₹120 crore and imports ₹70 crore, with investment ₹110 crore, government spending ₹140 crore and exports ₹60 crore. Compare leakages with injections.
(ii) Explain the likely effect on income and employment.
questions.solution_md: Injections exceed leakages; income and jobs rise.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Leakages = 90 + 120 + 70 = **₹280 crore**; injections = 110 + 140 + 60 = **₹310 crore**. Injections exceed leakages by **₹30 crore**.
(ii) Firms receive **more spending** than they paid out as income, so they **raise output** and **hire more workers**, and income rises. Rising income lifts saving, taxes and imports until leakages equal injections at a higher income.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain the circular flow of income in a four-sector economy, naming the flows between households, firms, the government and the rest of the world.
(ii) Imagined Vindhyadesh (₹ crore) has income 1,200, saving 160, taxes 240, imports 150, investment 180, government spending 260 and exports 110. Find consumption and show by two methods that its flow is in balance.
questions.solution_md: Flows among four sectors; consumption; two balance checks.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Households** supply factor services to firms and receive rent, wages, interest and profit, which they spend on consumer goods or save through the **financial market**, which lends to firms for **investment**. The **government** collects **taxes** from households and firms and returns money as **purchases**, **salaries**, **transfers** and **subsidies**. The **rest of the world** buys **exports**, sending money in, and sells **imports**, taking money out. So the leakages are saving, taxes and imports, and the injections are investment, government spending and exports.
(ii) Consumption = 1200 − 160 − 240 = **₹800 crore**. **Method 1**: leakages = 160 + 240 + 150 = ₹550 crore and injections = 180 + 260 + 110 = ₹550 crore, which are **equal**. **Method 2**: spending on domestic output = 800 + 180 + 260 + 110 − 150 = **₹1,200 crore**, equal to income. The flow is therefore in balance, and income will stay at this level.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain why national income settles where planned leakages equal planned injections, using the case where leakages are larger.
(ii) Imagined Pennarpur (₹ crore) has saving 130, taxes 170, investment 160, government spending 180 and exports 90. Find the imports that would keep its income steady, and evaluate whether cutting imports is a sound way to raise income.
questions.solution_md: Adjustment to balance; missing imports; balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) If planned **leakages exceed** planned injections, firms receive **less spending** than the income they paid out, so goods remain **unsold**. Firms **cut output** and employment, so **income falls**. As income falls, households save less, pay less tax and buy fewer imports, so **leakages shrink**. The fall stops when leakages have shrunk to equal injections. Only then is every rupee withdrawn returned as spending, so firms have no reason to change output and income **settles**.
(ii) Steady income needs S + T + M = I + G + X, so imports = 160 + 180 + 90 − 130 − 170 = **₹130 crore**. Cutting imports **reduces a leakage**, so more spending stays at home and income can rise. But many imports are **inputs** such as fuel and machines, and cutting them can **raise costs** and hurt production; other countries may also **buy fewer of our exports** in return, which cuts an injection. So import cuts help only in a limited way, and raising investment or exports is usually a sounder route.
